added_lemmas.statement: For a finite-dimensional convex body supplied with rationally encoded inner and outer radius bounds, polynomial-time weak membership and rational approximate-value oracles permit weak constrained convex-function minimization in oracle-polynomial time.  The output accuracy enters the running time through its logarithm; the returned point and value may be chosen rational.

source.locator: Theorem (4.3.13), pages 113--114, together with Definition (2.1.16), page 53, the oracle-polynomial convention on page 55, and Problem (2.1.22), page 56
source.verbatim_statement: Output: A vector \(y\in S(K,\varepsilon)\) such that \(f(y)<f(x)+\varepsilon\) for all \(x\in S(K,-\varepsilon)\).

attestation.note: Verified against the primary PDF at the stated locations. Theorem (4.3.13) takes a positive rational accuracy \(\varepsilon\), a centered convex body \((K;n,R,r,a_0)\) given by weak membership, and a globally defined convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) whose oracle, for rational \(x\) and positive rational \(\delta\), returns rational \(t\) with \(|f(x)-t|<\delta\). Definition (2.1.16) expands centeredness as rational data with \(B(a_0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(0,R)\). Problem (2.1.22) specifies that the returned vector is rational, and page 55 makes oracle-polynomial time polynomial in the body's rational encoding and the further inputs, hence logarithmic in inverse binary accuracy. The displayed output sentence is transcribed from Theorem (4.3.13), with notation normalized to LaTeX. One further call to the stated value oracle at the rational output supplies a rational approximate objective value to any requested rational accuracy.

sampling_model.overlap: The general endpoint, orbit-game, frontier, and compiler results allow every feasible count \(0\le r_{q,a}\le q\), including pure-control, pure-treatment, and label-constant menus. A local condition \(1\le r_{q,a}<q\) is used only to produce the higher-order observation obstruction for that realized cluster-label cell. The strict-separation and complement-symmetry specializations directly fix \(r_{3,1}=1\) and \(r_{3,2}=2\); their proofs check \(0<r_{3,a}<3\) and \(r_{3,1}\ne r_{3,2}\) from those displayed numbers and use no global interiority or saturation-variation assumption. Optimal designs may assign zero probability to labels or assignment orbits.

prose_updates.related_work: BairdBohrenMcIntoshOzler2018 provides the motivating fixed-count randomized-saturation design and its direct and spillover analysis, but not an unrestricted finite-population minimax estimator or a bit-certified joint design algorithm. AronowSamii2017 supplies exposure mappings, exposure-probability bookkeeping, and design-based estimation under general interference; the present paper instead optimizes jointly over every measurable estimator and every feasible correlated exact-count design. HudgensHalloran2008, BasseFeller2018, and JiangImaiMalani2023 develop the design-based two-stage causal framework without the present all-estimator finite saddle characterization. Bai2023 proves complete randomization by permutation-invariance group averaging for a fixed invariant estimator; here group averaging reduces the entire design--estimator--nature game and retains arbitrary correlated saturation actions. CaiPougetAbadieAiroldi2022 optimizes randomized and deterministic saturation designs for a specified difference-in-means estimator under linear interference, whereas the present criterion is worst-case finite-population squared error over all bounded schedules and all measurable estimators. Kallus2021 establishes mixed-strategy design optimality at a general decision-theoretic level, while the present result constructs and weakly optimizes the exact rational observation-hypergraph quotient. The accepted-bank paper \texttt{exp\_multiarm\_secondorder\_minimax\_frontier\_v1} supplies the finite unrestricted response-orbit minimax and rational-program certificate architecture in the no-interference setting. The present paper inherits that finite minimax architecture, but adds the exact-count higher-order observation hypergraph, the quotient of arbitrary correlated saturation-label actions, the stabilizer-weighted exact kernel, the conditional-uniformity reduction, and a total zero-face-safe decoder with a bit-certified compiler. Hull2026 and SudijonoDobribanTchetgenTchetgen2026 supply endpoint reductions in no-interference experiments, whereas the present compiler covers bounded anonymous saturation interference, arbitrary correlated first-stage laws, boundary treated counts, and label-constant menus. KandirosHarshawSavje2026 studies a pairwise conflict-graph experiment; here every interior exact-count cell yields \(h+1\) same-arm coordinates whose \(h\)-subsets are all observable although the full set is not, so no pairwise graph represents the compatibility complex.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The compiler guarantee is polynomial in the displayed orbit-program size for fixed \(K\) and \(b\); it does not make the constant-size response alphabet small in practice and is not a strongly polynomial algorithm. Exact rational arithmetic may produce large certificates even though their bit length is polynomial. The numerical size-three witness remains supported by its separate exhaustive rational verifier, while the compiler theorem supplies the general symbolic kernel construction, global oracle geometry, erosion-correct weak optimization, tolerance accounting, and decoder proof rather than a new numerical rerun. The strict separation is a finite-game, contrast-neighborhood result; no topology on observable laws or asymptotic experiment sequence is part of the theorem.
prose_updates.honest_scope: Endpoint completeness, the exact orbit game, and the bit-certified compiler cover every rational feasible table \(0\le r_{q,a}\le q\), including pure-control, pure-treatment, and label-constant treated-count menus. Hypergraph nonrepresentability is local: it follows whenever a realized cluster-label cell has \(1\le r_{q,a}<q\), with no claim for a table consisting only of boundary cells. The independent-saturation result is a finite primal-dual feasibility and positive-support saddle characterization, not an elementary closed-form classification. The compiler returns rational weakly optimal certificates and a total continuous estimator; it does not claim exact rational optimizers or a separation as the number of clusters tends to infinity. The strict advantage is only the certified two-cluster exact-count game and its stated infinite rational contrast neighborhood. It does not claim robustness in an ambient observable-law topology, nondegenerate superpopulation conditional support or variance, positive region mass, or asymptotic persistence; those would be different strengthening projects, not premises of the stated finite minimax inequality.

proofs.proof_tex:
We divide the proof into endpoint completion, symmetry reduction, construction of the orbit kernel, and minimax duality.

First, \(\sum_{z,a}c_{z,a}=0\) implies
\[
 \sum_{z,a:c_{z,a}>0}c_{z,a}
 =-\sum_{z,a:c_{z,a}<0}c_{z,a}
 ={1\over2}\sum_{z,a}|c_{z,a}|=L.
\]
Together with \(0\le Y_{gi}(z,a)\le1\) from \(\texttt{ass:bounded-outcomes}\), this proves \(|\tau(Y)|\le L\), so clipping an estimator to \([-L,L]\) cannot increase squared error.

Fix a design \(D\) and an endpoint table \(d\).  For a complete \(y\in\mathcal M\), independently draw every coordinate
\[
 B_{gi}(z,a)\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(y_{gi}(z,a)).                       \tag{5}
\]
The restriction of (5) to \(\mathcal O(x)\) is exactly the conditional Bernoulli experiment in \(\texttt{def:endpoint-extension}\).  Linearity of \(\tau\) gives \(\mathbb E_B\tau(B)=\tau(y)\).  Therefore, for every assignment \(x\),
\[
 \overline d(x,y|_{\mathcal O(x)})-\tau(y)
 =\mathbb E_B\!\left[d(x,B|_{\mathcal O(x)})-\tau(B)\right].             \tag{6}
\]
For \(Z=d(x,B|_{\mathcal O(x)})-\tau(B)\), the identity
\(\mathbb E_B[Z^2]-(\mathbb E_B Z)^2
=\mathbb E_B[(Z-\mathbb E_B Z)^2]\ge0\) proves the required quadratic Jensen
inequality directly.  Applying it in (6), followed by expectation over
\(X\sim D\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R(D,\overline d;y)
 &\le \mathbb E_B\mathcal R(D,d;B)\\
 &\le \max_{b_0\in\mathcal M\cap\{0,1\}^{2KN}}
            \mathcal R(D,d;b_0).
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{7}
\]
This proves the displayed extension inequality.  Restricting nature from the cube to its vertices gives the reverse minimax inequality.  Taking the infimum over endpoint tables in (7) consequently proves endpoint equivalence, first for every fixed \(D\), and then after minimizing over \(D\).  The finite endpoint decision cube is compact, so the endpoint minimizer is attained.

Now enlarge the group in the preceding lemma to \(\Gamma\), also allowing
permutations of equal-size clusters.  The model cube, assignment set,
observation relation, and scalar target are invariant.  To make the averaging
step explicit, choose \(\gamma\) uniformly in \(\Gamma\), apply the transformed
design--rule pair \((\gamma D,\gamma\delta)\), and then forget \(\gamma\).
Invariance makes its risk at \(Y\) the average of the original risks at
\(\gamma^{-1}Y\), hence no larger than the original worst-case risk.  Conditional
on the realized data, replace the resulting randomized decision by its
conditional mean.  The conditional identity
\[
 \mathbb E[(Z-\theta)^2\mid X,V]
 =\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid X,V)
  +(\mathbb E[Z\mid X,V]-\theta)^2
\]
shows that this replacement cannot increase squared risk.  Thus an invariant
procedure is no worse in maximum risk; this is the equal-size-cluster extension
of the unit-permutation argument in
\(\texttt{lem:conditional-uniformity}\).  If \(B(\Pi)\) denotes the minimum
Bayes risk under a prior \(\Pi\) on binary schedules, then \(B\) is concave,
because it is an infimum of functions linear in \(\Pi\).  Hence
\[
 B\!\left({1\over|\Gamma|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\gamma\Pi\right)
 \ge {1\over|\Gamma|}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}B(\gamma\Pi)=B(\Pi).       \tag{8}
\]
Thus both players may be restricted to invariant strategies.

Let \(h_0=2^{2K}\).  A binary unit response is one of \(h_0\) complete \(2K\)-bit vectors.  Consequently a size-\(q\) cluster response type is a multiset of \(q\) such vectors, and their number is
\[
 B_q=\binom{q+h_0-1}{h_0-1}=\binom{q+h_0-1}{q}.                             \tag{9}
\]
An invariant global response is the size-tagged histogram \(\kappa\) of these cluster types.  An invariant assignment is the histogram \(n=(n_{q,a})\).  Conditional uniformity shows that, given \(n\), labels are allocated uniformly among equal-size clusters and the treated subsets are then independent and uniform.  For label \(a\), a local binary observation is the triple \((a,u,v)\), with
\[
 0\le u\le r_{q,a},\; 0\le v\le q-r_{q,a};                               \tag{10}
\]
there are \(O_q=\sum_a(r_{q,a}+1)(q-r_{q,a}+1)\) such triples.  Notice that the response type in (9) retains the joint \(2K\)-bit vector of each unit; no pairwise-conflict or marginal-total replacement has been made.

For a fixed cluster response type \(t\), direct counting under uniform exact-count sampling gives precisely the rational probability \(P_{t,a}(u,v)\) in \(\texttt{def:local-kernel}\).  Expanding
\[
 F_{\kappa,q}(z)=\prod_t
 \left(\sum_{a,u,v}P_{t,a}(u,v)z_{a,u,v}\right)^{\kappa_{q,t}}             \tag{11}
\]
sums the product probabilities over all assignments of local observation triples to the clusters represented by \(\kappa\).  The coefficient of \(z^{\omega_q}\) retains exactly those allocations having observation histogram \(\omega_q\).  If its label margins are \((n_{q,a})_a\), there are
\(
 \binom{m_q}{(n_{q,a})_a}
\)
equally likely allocations of those labels.  Division by this number and multiplication over cluster sizes proves
\[
 \Pr\{\omega\mid\kappa,n\}=H_{\kappa n\omega}.                            \tag{12}
\]
For incompatible margins the probability is zero.  Substituting every \(z_{a,u,v}=1\) in (11) shows that the compatible coefficients sum to the multinomial denominator, and hence
\[
 H_{\kappa n\omega}\ge0,\; \sum_{\omega}H_{\kappa n\omega}=1.           \tag{13}
\]
The argument remains valid at \(r_{q,a}=0,q\): the unique subset has probability one and (10) merely has a singleton range in one coordinate.  A label-constant treated-count menu likewise creates no division by zero.  Since the local denominators are positive integers and \(c\) is rational, (11)--(13) also prove that both \(H\) and \(\theta\) are rational.

As an independent smallest heterogeneous stress test, take sizes \((3,3,4)\), counts \((r_{3,1},r_{3,2})=(1,2)\), \((r_{4,1},r_{4,2})=(1,3)\), size-three response types \((0,1,3)\), \((2,12,15)\), and size-four response type \((0,1,6,15)\), where an integer records the low-to-high response bits in order \((1,1),(0,1),(1,2),(0,2)\).  Direct labeled enumeration over every label allocation and every feasible subset agrees cell by cell with (11)--(12) for all six assignment histograms.  In lexicographic order of the two label-one counts \((n_{3,1},n_{4,1})\), their support sizes are \(6,8,27,36,24,32\), and each of the six rational rows sums exactly to one.  This check uses the full observation histograms, not pairwise conflicts.

Write \(d_n\) for invariant design mass, \(\delta_{n\omega}\in[-L,L]\), and \(t_{n\omega}=d_n\delta_{n\omega}\).  By (12), the risk against response orbit \(\kappa\) is
\[
 r_\kappa(d,t)=\sum_{n,\omega}H_{\kappa n\omega}
       {\bigl(t_{n\omega}-d_n\theta_\kappa\bigr)^2\over d_n}.             \tag{14}
\]
At \(d_n=0\), the bounds \(|t_{n\omega}|\le Ld_n\) force \(t_{n\omega}=0\), and the closed perspective in (14) is zero.  Indeed, writing \(t=d\delta\) shows that each summand is \(dH(\delta-\theta)^2\), which converges uniformly to zero as \(d\downarrow0\).  Thus (14) is a continuous convex function on the compact set
\[
 \mathcal C=\{(d,t):d\ge0,\ \sum_nd_n=1,\ |t_{n\omega}|\le Ld_n\}.         \tag{15}
\]
Minimizing \(\max_\kappa r_\kappa\) over (15) is exactly \(\mathsf P\), so its value is attained.

For \(\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal K)\), apply the cited compact minimax theorem \(\texttt{lem:sion-compact-minimax}\) to
\[
 F((d,t),\pi)=\sum_\kappa\pi_\kappa r_\kappa(d,t)                         \tag{16}
\]
on the two compact convex sets (15) and \(\Delta(\mathcal K)\).  By (14), (16) is continuous and convex in \((d,t)\), and it is linear, hence concave, in \(\pi\).  The theorem gives
\[
 \min_{(d,t)\in\mathcal C}\max_\kappa r_\kappa(d,t)
 =\max_{\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal K)}\min_{(d,t)\in\mathcal C}F((d,t),\pi). \tag{17}
\]
For fixed \(\pi,n,\omega\), completing the square gives
\[
 \sum_\kappa\pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}
       (\delta-\theta_\kappa)^2
 =a_{n\omega}\left(\delta-{h_{n\omega}\over a_{n\omega}}\right)^2
  +\sum_\kappa\pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}\theta_\kappa^2
  -{h_{n\omega}^2\over a_{n\omega}}                                      \tag{18}
\]
when \(a_{n\omega}>0\).  The ratio \(h/a\) is a convex combination of values in \([-L,L]\), so it is feasible.  When \(a_{n\omega}=0\), nonnegativity implies every \(\pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}=0\), hence also \(h_{n\omega}=0\), and the whole cell contributes zero for every clipped decision.  Summing (18) over \(\omega\), then minimizing over \(d\), yields
\[
 \min_{(d,t)\in\mathcal C}F((d,t),\pi)=\min_{n\in\mathcal N}b_n(\pi).     \tag{19}
\]
Equations (17)--(19) are exactly \(\operatorname{val}(\mathsf P)=\operatorname{val}(\mathsf Q)=R^\star\).  Compactness and continuity give attainment on both sides.  Equation (18) supplies the posterior-mean rule on every positive-mass cell and proves that every value in \([-L,L]\) is valid on a zero-mass cell.

Finally, the three orbit counts are
\[
 \prod_{q=3}^b\binom{m_q+B_q-1}{B_q-1},\;
 \prod_{q=3}^b\binom{m_q+K-1}{K-1},\;
 \prod_{q=3}^b\binom{m_q+O_q-1}{O_q-1}.                                   \tag{20}
\]
The elementary bounds \(B_q\le h_0^q\le2^{2Kb}\), \(O_q\le K2^q\le K2^b\), and \(m_q\le m\), with fixed \(K,b\), turn the product of (20) and its kernel indices into
\(
 (m+1)^{O(2^{2Kb}+K2^b)}
\)
entries.  To implement an optimal \(d\), draw \(n\), allocate its labels uniformly to equal-size labeled clusters, and draw the exact-count subsets independently and uniformly.  Equation (12) proves that this realizes the optimized orbit experiment, and \(\texttt{lem:conditional-uniformity}\) proves that no nonuniform second-stage law can improve it.

The two prescribed counts satisfy the local numerical conditions
\[
1\le r_{3,1}=1<3,
\qquad
1\le r_{3,2}=2<3,
\qquad
r_{3,1}\ne r_{3,2}.
\]
These inequalities and the variation condition follow directly from the theorem's displayed instance; no condition on any other entry of \(r\) is used.  The coefficient vector has zero sum, and
\[
L={1\over2}(3+1+1+1)=3.                                                    \tag{1}
\]
Thus this is an admissible instance of the exact binary orbit game supplied by \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\).  In particular, every upper bound computed below for all binary response orbits is also an upper bound over the full bounded schedule class \(\mathcal M\), and every binary prior below is a valid lower bound over \(\mathcal M\).

We first reconstruct the finite likelihood table.  Encode a unit's four binary responses, in the order \((1,1),(0,1),(1,2),(0,2)\), as the four low-to-high bits of an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,15\}\).  A size-three cluster type is a nondecreasing triple of such integers.  Hence the number of cluster types and the number of unordered two-cluster response orbits are, respectively,
\[
T=\binom{16+3-1}{3}=816,
\qquad
\binom{T+1}{2}=333336.                                                       \tag{2}
\]
For a cluster type \(t\), let \(C_{a,t,k}\) be the number of the three feasible exact-count subsets at label \(a\) that produce local observation index \(k\).  At label one put \(k=3u+v\), where \(u\) and \(v\) are the treated-one and control-one counts; at label two put \(k=2u+v\).  In both cases \(0\le k<6\), and the local kernel in \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\) is
\[
P_{t,a}(k)={C_{a,t,k}\over3},
\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{5}C_{a,t,k}=3.                                                  \tag{3}
\]

Order the observation cells by the upper triangle for assignment orbit \(11\), the \(6\)-by-\(6\) rectangle for orbit \(12\), and the upper triangle for orbit \(22\).  For an unordered response orbit \(\{t,t'\}\), define its integer likelihood row by
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_{tt',\{k,l\}_{11}}
 &=2\left(C_{1,t,k}C_{1,t',l}
       +\mathbf 1\{k<l\}C_{1,t,l}C_{1,t',k}\right), && k\le l,\\
M_{tt',(k,l)_{12}}
 &=C_{1,t,k}C_{2,t',l}+C_{1,t',k}C_{2,t,l}, &&0\le k,l<6,\\
M_{tt',\{k,l\}_{22}}
 &=2\left(C_{2,t,k}C_{2,t',l}
       +\mathbf 1\{k<l\}C_{2,t,l}C_{2,t',k}\right), && k\le l.
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{4}
\]
For blocks \(11\) and \(22\), summing the upper-triangular symmetrization in (4) gives twice the sum over all ordered pairs of local indices; by (3) it is \(2\cdot3\cdot3=18\).  The rectangular block also sums to \(3\cdot3+3\cdot3=18\).  Therefore
\[
H_{\{t,t'\},g,j}={M_{tt',j}\over18},
\qquad
\sum_{j:g(j)=g}H_{\{t,t'\},g,j}=1                                        \tag{5}
\]
for each \(g\in\{11,12,22\}\).  The two terms in the middle line of (4) are exactly the two equally likely label orientations in orbit \(12\); the factor two in the same-label blocks gives the corresponding unordered-observation normalization.  Thus (4), not a pairwise-conflict surrogate, is the exact observation-hypergraph kernel.

As a separate normalization stress test for the same coefficient construction, take cluster sizes \((3,3,4)\), counts \((r_{3,1},r_{3,2})=(1,2)\) and \((r_{4,1},r_{4,2})=(1,3)\), size-three response types \((0,1,3)\), \((2,12,15)\), and size-four response type \((0,1,6,15)\).  Expanding the local kernels and, independently, enumerating every labeled label allocation and feasible treated subset give identical rational probabilities in every observation-histogram cell.  In lexicographic order of \((n_{3,1},n_{4,1})\in\{0,1,2\}\times\{0,1\}\), the six row support sizes are
\[
6, 8, 27, 36, 24, 32,                                                  \tag{6}
\]
and every row sums exactly to one.  This verifies the assignment-orbit divisor at the heterogeneous-size boundary before the specialized certificate is used.

We next give the unrestricted primal certificate.  Put
\[
(q_{11},q_{12},q_{22})={1\over10^8}(50372138,42844038,6783824),              \tag{7}
\]
whose coordinates are positive and sum to one.  In the cell order preceding (4), set \(d_j=e_j/10^5\), where
\[
\begin{split}
(e_j)_{j=0}^{77}={}&(-78795,-99673,-125925,42873,13619,-28110,-131707,-161503,
21409,0,-22496,-189980,0,-21409,-43058,189980,161503,123041,131707,100384,81531,\\
&47551,0,-31307,-33852,-14286,-109350,21499,-22463,-30459,-80795,-69654,-145451,5723,
-93539,-52330,-155278,-89207,-178491,178491,71330,171200,14818,67123,-5722,\\
&145451,90301,68712,21192,47169,-21499,134172,-16612,102456,-11008,6753,-51501,
165520,114346,101636,42573,20700,0,65736,36413,50311,0,-93454,-33333,-33333,\\
&33333,-62461,1415,-49421,-150652,0,9511,-165520).
\end{split}                                                                 \tag{8}
\]
Every decision in (8) belongs to \([-3,3]\), so (1) proves clipping feasibility.  For a cluster type \(t\), define the integer
\[
T(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\left(3Y_i(1,1)-Y_i(0,1)-Y_i(1,2)-Y_i(0,2)\right).       \tag{9}
\]
The target at response orbit \(\{t,t'\}\) is \((T(t)+T(t'))/6\), and its numerator \(h=T(t)+T(t')\) lies in \([-18,18]\).

For cell \(j\), let \(g(j)\) denote its assignment block, and define the integer outward rounding
\[
A_{h,j}=\left\lceil
10^9q_{g(j)}{(6e_j-10^5h)^2\over(6\cdot10^5)^2}
\right\rceil.                                                              \tag{10}
\]
Consequently
\[
q_{g(j)}\left(d_j-{h\over6}\right)^2\le {A_{h,j}\over10^9}.              \tag{11}
\]
Enumerate cluster types lexicographically as all triples \(0\le j_1\le j_2\le j_3\le15\), enumerate their upper-triangular pairs, construct (3)--(4), and use integer ceiling division in (10).  This exhaustive integer calculation gives
\[
\max_{t\le t'}{1\over18\cdot10^9}
 \sum_{j=0}^{77}M_{tt',j}A_{T(t)+T(t'),j}
 ={682490711\over500000000}.                                                \tag{12}
\]
All operations in (12) are integer additions, multiplications, divisions with remainder, and a maximum over the \(333336\) orbits in (2).  Combining (5), (11), and (12) proves
\[
R^\star\le {682490711\over500000000}=1.364981422.                          \tag{13}
\]

For the dual certificate, put the displayed numerator divided by \(9999999\) on each response orbit below:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|r}
t&t'&\text{numerator}\\ \hline
(0,0,3)&(13,13,13)&93579\\
(0,1,3)&(0,1,3)&32185\\
(0,1,3)&(0,3,3)&4627\\
(0,1,3)&(1,1,1)&1175451\\
(0,3,3)&(0,3,3)&1277354\\
(0,3,3)&(13,13,13)&937059\\
(1,1,1)&(1,1,1)&704115\\
(2,2,2)&(2,2,2)&501848\\
(2,2,2)&(12,12,15)&937061\\
(2,2,2)&(12,15,15)&93580\\
(2,2,2)&(13,13,13)&547561\\
(12,12,15)&(12,12,15)&1277355\\
(12,12,15)&(12,14,15)&4624\\
(12,14,15)&(12,14,15)&32186\\
(12,14,15)&(14,14,14)&1175451\\
(13,13,13)&(13,13,13)&501848\\
(14,14,14)&(14,14,14)&704115
\end{array}                                                                 \tag{14}
\]
The numerators sum to \(9999999\), so (14) is a rational prior.  For completeness, if its orbit weights are \(w_\kappa\), define, in cell \(j\),
\[
s_{rj}=\sum_\kappa w_\kappa H_{\kappa,g(j),j}\theta_\kappa^r,
\qquad r=0,1,2.                                                            \tag{15}
\]
Completing the square gives the minimum conditional squared loss in that cell as
\[
s_{2j}-{s_{1j}^2\over s_{0j}}                                               \tag{16}
\]
when \(s_{0j}>0\).  When \(s_{0j}=0\), nonnegativity of every summand in (15) forces \(s_{1j}=s_{2j}=0\), and the contribution is defined to be zero.  Thus (16) treats every zero-likelihood face without division.  Summing (16) within the three assignment blocks and substituting (4), (9), and (14) yields
\[
\begin{split}
B_{11}&={15375502988468197921840146383881271727233984862425002228885431140677343747
\over11264307876254729959135311641689644340133922991873868807613042371771565600},\\
B_{12}&={448449106336744246211520343854236088916292823478774594883
\over328540052093168094561750909236330942644710693505276887705},\\
B_{22}&={875407001549306027053357121
\over641335093640491500999272160}.
\end{split}                                                                 \tag{17}
\]
Direct positive-denominator cross multiplication in (17) gives
\[
B_{11}>{13649753\over10^7},
\qquad B_{12}>{13649753\over10^7},
\qquad B_{22}>{13649753\over10^7}.                                         \tag{18}
\]
For any design and any estimator, its maximum risk is at least its average risk under (14).  Conditional on an observed assignment block, (15)--(16) is the minimum of that average risk over every, possibly nonlinear, decision rule.  The design's Bayes risk is therefore at least the convex combination of the three numbers in (17), hence at least their minimum.  Taking the infimum over designs and estimators and using (18) proves
\[
R^\star>{13649753\over10^7}=1.3649753.                                     \tag{19}
\]
Equations (13) and (19) have certificate gap
\[
{682490711\over500000000}-{13649753\over10^7}
={3061\over500000000}<10^{-5}.                                             \tag{20}
\]

We now certify the lower bound for every common-probability independent-saturation design.  Put the displayed numerator divided by \(10000001\) on each response orbit below:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|r}
t&t'&\text{numerator}\\ \hline
(0,1,3)&(0,1,3)&22021\\
(0,1,3)&(1,1,1)&1206305\\
(0,2,3)&(13,13,13)&96393\\
(0,3,3)&(0,3,3)&1290697\\
(0,3,3)&(13,13,13)&922076\\
(1,1,1)&(1,1,1)&693092\\
(2,2,2)&(2,2,2)&570855\\
(2,2,2)&(12,12,15)&922076\\
(2,2,2)&(12,13,15)&96391\\
(2,2,2)&(13,13,13)&397129\\
(12,12,15)&(12,12,15)&1290696\\
(12,14,15)&(12,14,15)&22012\\
(12,14,15)&(14,14,14)&1206312\\
(13,13,13)&(13,13,13)&570855\\
(14,14,14)&(14,14,14)&693091
\end{array}                                                                 \tag{21}
\]
The numerators in (21) sum to \(10000001\).  Applying (15)--(16) to this prior gives the exact conditional Bayes risks
\[
\begin{split}
b_0&={510475303939035976629005312819976017636302495199788360789626523726439
\over369944115755171414919449929497305596423215368453011019149630652456016},\\
b_1&={1481174023898820321516133538462560606861100123434633
\over1112403418358068410799836111119084211132456048612006},\\
b_2&={151645559092055579448236753
\over104500605048826858776739890},
\end{split}                                                                 \tag{22}
\]
for blocks \(11,12,22\), respectively.  If \(p\in[0,1]\) is the common probability of label one, the three observed assignment-orbit probabilities are \(p^2\), \(2p(1-p)\), and \((1-p)^2\).  Because the realized assignment is part of the data, minimization over all decisions separates across these three blocks.  Hence the exact Bayes risk under (21) is
\[
q(p)=b_0p^2+2b_1p(1-p)+b_2(1-p)^2.                                        \tag{23}
\]
This identity remains literal at \(p=0\) and \(p=1\); the zero-mass assignment cells then contribute zero and impose no posterior division.

Set \(A=b_0-2b_1+b_2\).  Exact cross multiplication of the positive denominators in (22) gives
\[
A>0,
\qquad
0<{b_2-b_1\over A}<1.                                                       \tag{24}
\]
Thus the quadratic minimizer lies in the probability interval, and completing the square gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{0\le p\le1}q(p)
 &=b_2-{(b_2-b_1)^2\over A}\\
 &={15905203453139106542517135433476445901965288230411009200606834963558543472086380998618525138518327606158980351835088763299728100108165337352676095029503340442637423716141827041
\over11644070726222582883296696074226046164046332571505009828610177241754496145584750907986901385009654041984574087952923135008216678502549249251959833183001560101499077844672521234}\\
 &>{13659\over10000}.
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{25}
\]
For each fixed \(p\), the maximum risk of every estimator is at least its average risk under (21), whose infimum over all measurable estimators is (23).  Infimizing also over \(p\) and using (25) proves
\[
R_{\mathrm{ind}}>{13659\over10000}=1.3659.                                \tag{26}
\]
This lower bound covers every nonlinear estimator and the entire closed interval of independent assignment probabilities, not a grid or an interior restriction.  Combining (13) and (26) gives
\[
R_{\mathrm{ind}}-R^\star
>{13659\over10000}-{682490711\over500000000}
={459289\over500000000}=0.000918578.                                      \tag{27}
\]
In view of \(\texttt{thm:independence-frontier}\), (27) also certifies that the finite independent-saturation saddle system is infeasible for this instance; in particular no omitted positive-support equality can restore equality of the two minimax values.

It remains to prove the contrast-neighborhood statement.  Let \(\alpha\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy \(|\alpha|\le10^{-5}\), and let \(\tau_\alpha\) be the target for coefficient vector \((3+\alpha,-1-\alpha,-1,-1)\).  The signs of the four coefficients do not change on this interval, their sum remains zero, and the contrast remains admissible.  Since \(N=6\), \(\texttt{ass:bounded-outcomes}\) gives, for every fixed schedule,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\tau_\alpha(Y)-\tau_0(Y)|
&=\left|{\alpha\over6}\sum_{g,i}
       \{Y_{gi}(1,1)-Y_{gi}(0,1)\}\right|\\
&\le |\alpha|.                                                             
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{28}
\]

For either the unrestricted design class or the common-probability independent class, write its minimax risk at contrast \(\alpha\) as \(R_{\mathcal D,\alpha}\).  We may perform the following comparison over the common class of all real-valued measurable estimators: because \(\tau_\alpha(Y)\) belongs to its bounded target interval, projection of any decision onto that interval weakly decreases its pointwise squared error.  Thus allowing all real decisions does not alter the clipped minimax value.

For a fixed design, estimator, and schedule, put \(E_0=\delta(X,V)-\tau_0(Y)\) and \(h=\tau_0(Y)-\tau_\alpha(Y)\).  The elementary variance identity gives \(|\mathbb E_D E_0|\le(\mathbb E_D E_0^2)^{1/2}\), because \(\mathbb E_D[(E_0-\mathbb E_D E_0)^2]\ge0\).  Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
\{\mathbb E_D(E_0+h)^2\}^{1/2}
&\le \{\mathbb E_D E_0^2
       +2|h|(\mathbb E_D E_0^2)^{1/2}+h^2\}^{1/2}\\
&=(\mathbb E_D E_0^2)^{1/2}+|h|.
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{29}
\]
Taking the supremum over schedules, then the infimum over designs and estimators, and using (28) yields
\[
\sqrt{R_{\mathcal D,\alpha}}
\le\sqrt{R_{\mathcal D,0}}+|\alpha|.                                     \tag{30}
\]
Interchanging \(0\) and \(\alpha\) in the same argument proves
\[
\left|\sqrt{R_{\mathcal D,\alpha}}
      -\sqrt{R_{\mathcal D,0}}\right|\le|\alpha|.                        \tag{31}
\]

Put \(a=\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{ind},0}}\) and \(b=\sqrt{R^\star_0}\).  The zero decision and (1) give \(a,b\le3\), while (26) gives \(a>1>|\alpha|\).  Therefore (27) and (31) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathrm{ind},\alpha}-R^\star_\alpha
&\ge(a-|\alpha|)^2-(b+|\alpha|)^2\\
&=a^2-b^2-2|\alpha|(a+b)\\
&>0.000918578-12|\alpha|\\
&\ge0.000798578>7\times10^{-4}.
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{32}
\]
Every rational \(\alpha\) in the stated interval preserves rationality and the zero-sum contrast condition.  Equations (13), (19), (20), (26), (27), and (32) prove every claimed certificate and the infinite rational contrast neighborhood.

This is a self-contained finite design-based separation inside the exact-count game: randomness is only the assignment law, the potential-outcome schedule is fixed, and the robustness statement varies only the rational contrast.  No ambient observable-law topology, superpopulation support or variance condition, region-mass condition, or asymptotic persistence assertion is used or implied.

For \(p\in\Delta(\mathcal A)\), independence of the cluster labels with their common law \(p\), followed by conditionally independent uniform exact-count subset randomization, gives the assignment-orbit probability
\[
d_n(p)=\prod_{q=3}^{b}
 \binom{m_q}{(n_{q,a})_{a\in\mathcal A}}
 \prod_{a\in\mathcal A}p_a^{n_{q,a}},
\qquad n\in\mathcal N,                                                     \tag{31}
\]
where \(0^0=1\).  Every factor in (31) is a monomial, including on a face of \(\Delta(\mathcal A)\), and the multinomial theorem gives \(\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}d_n(p)=1\).

For a clipped orbit decision table \(\delta=(\delta_{n\omega})\), define its risk at response orbit \(\kappa\) by
\[
 \rho_\kappa(p,\delta)
 :=\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}\sum_{\omega\in\mathcal W}
 d_n(p)H_{\kappa n\omega}
 \bigl(\delta_{n\omega}-\theta_\kappa\bigr)^2.                            \tag{32}
\]
The endpoint and orbit equivalence in \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\), applied to the independent design whose orbit law is (31), yields
\[
 R_{\mathrm{ind}}
 =\min_{p\in\Delta(\mathcal A),\,
              \delta\in[-L,L]^{\mathcal N\times\mathcal W}}
       \max_{\kappa\in\mathcal K}\rho_\kappa(p,\delta).                 \tag{33}
\]
This minimum is attained: both displayed decision sets are compact, each \(d_n(p)\) is continuous by (31), each \(\rho_\kappa\) is continuous by the finite sum (32), and a finite maximum of continuous functions is continuous.

Suppose first that \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}=R^\star=:v\).  Choose an attaining restricted pair \((p,\delta)\) in (33).  Then
\[
 \rho_\kappa(p,\delta)\le v
 \quad\text{for every }\kappa\in\mathcal K.                               \tag{34}
\]
By the strong minimax equality and dual attainment proved in \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\), there is an attaining \(\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal K)\) such that
\[
 \min_{n\in\mathcal N}b_n(\pi)=R^\star=v,
 \quad\text{and hence}\quad
 b_n(\pi)\ge v\quad\text{for every }n\in\mathcal N.                     \tag{35}
\]
Equations (34)--(35), together with the simplex conditions and clipping already imposed in (33), are exactly the two inequality families and the domain constraints in \(\texttt{def:independence-feasibility-system}\).  Thus that finite system is feasible.

Conversely, let \((p,\delta,\pi,v)\) satisfy \(\texttt{def:independence-feasibility-system}\).  Its first inequality family and (33) imply \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}\le v\).  Its second family gives \(\min_n b_n(\pi)\ge v\), so weak duality for the dual game in \(\texttt{def:dual-game}\), or equivalently the primal--dual equality in \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\), gives \(R^\star\ge v\).  Because every common-probability independent design is an admissible unrestricted design, the two infima satisfy \(R^\star\le R_{\mathrm{ind}}\).  Consequently
\[
 R_{\mathrm{ind}}\le v\le R^\star\le R_{\mathrm{ind}},
 \qquad \text{so}\qquad
 R_{\mathrm{ind}}=R^\star=v.                                               \tag{36}
\]
This proves both directions of the finite feasibility characterization.

We next derive all positive-support equalities for an arbitrary feasible tuple.  Write
\[
 a_{n\omega}:=\sum_{\kappa\in\mathcal K}
                  \pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega},
 \qquad
 h_{n\omega}:=\sum_{\kappa\in\mathcal K}
                  \pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}\theta_\kappa.           \tag{37}
\]
Since \(H\) is the probability kernel furnished by \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\), \(H_{\kappa n\omega}\ge0\) and \(\sum_\omega H_{\kappa n\omega}=1\).  Expanding the squares in (32), summing with weights \(\pi_\kappa\), and then completing the square on each cell having \(a_{n\omega}>0\), gives, for every \(n\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 B_n(\delta;\pi)
 &:=\sum_{\kappa\in\mathcal K}\pi_\kappa
       \sum_{\omega\in\mathcal W}H_{\kappa n\omega}
       (\delta_{n\omega}-\theta_\kappa)^2 \\
 &= b_n(\pi)
   +\sum_{\omega:\,a_{n\omega}>0}a_{n\omega}
      \left(\delta_{n\omega}-\frac{h_{n\omega}}{a_{n\omega}}\right)^2.
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{38}
\]
There is no division on a zero-likelihood face: if \(a_{n\omega}=0\), nonnegativity of the summands in (37) implies
\(\pi_\kappa H_{\kappa n\omega}=0\) for every \(\kappa\), whence \(h_{n\omega}=0\) and the cell contributes zero to the first line of (38).  If \(a_{n\omega}>0\), the ratio \(h_{n\omega}/a_{n\omega}\) is a convex combination of values \(\theta_\kappa\in[-L,L]\), and therefore it is itself in \([-L,L]\).

Average the primal feasibility inequalities (34) with the prior weights and use (38).  The dual feasibility inequalities and \(\sum_n d_n(p)=1\) then give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v
 &\ge \sum_{\kappa\in\mathcal K}\pi_\kappa
          \rho_\kappa(p,\delta) \\
 &=\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}d_n(p)b_n(\pi)
   +\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}\sum_{\omega:\,a_{n\omega}>0}
       d_n(p)a_{n\omega}
       \left(\delta_{n\omega}-\frac{h_{n\omega}}{a_{n\omega}}\right)^2 \\
 &\ge\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}d_n(p)b_n(\pi)
 \ge\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}d_n(p)v=v.
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{39}
\]
Thus every inequality in (39) is an equality.

First, the final equality and the nonnegative quantities \(d_n(p)(b_n(\pi)-v)\) show that
\[
 d_n(p)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b_n(\pi)=v.                            \tag{40}
\]
Second, the middle nonnegative sum in (39) vanishes term by term, so
\[
 d_n(p)a_{n\omega}>0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \delta_{n\omega}=\frac{h_{n\omega}}{a_{n\omega}}.                       \tag{41}
\]
This is the posterior-mean decision on every observation cell having positive joint design--prior likelihood.  If \(d_n(p)=0\), the cell never occurs under the independent design and its clipped decision has no effect on any risk in (32).  If \(d_n(p)>0\) but \(a_{n\omega}=0\), the cell has zero likelihood under \(\pi\), its term in (38) is identically zero, and no posterior-mean equality is imposed; its table entry can be any value in \([-L,L]\) compatible with the primal feasibility inequalities.  This treats all zero-probability faces without forming \(h_{n\omega}/a_{n\omega}\).

Finally, equality of the first and last lines of (39) yields
\[
 0=v-\sum_{\kappa\in\mathcal K}\pi_\kappa\rho_\kappa(p,\delta)
   =\sum_{\kappa\in\mathcal K}\pi_\kappa
        \bigl(v-\rho_\kappa(p,\delta)\bigr).                              \tag{42}
\]
Every summand in (42) is nonnegative by primal feasibility.  Hence the complementary positive-response-support condition is
\[
 \pi_\kappa>0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \rho_\kappa(p,\delta)=v.                                                  \tag{43}
\]
Equations (40), (41), and (43) are respectively the positive assignment-support, positive observation-likelihood, and positive least-favorable-response-support saddle equalities.  Together with (36), they prove the claimed full finite primal--dual characterization without imposing interiority of \(p\) or asserting a closed-form classification.

proposed.statement: For two size-three clusters, \(K=2\), \(r_{3,1}=1\), \(r_{3,2}=2\), and coefficient order \((c_{1,1},c_{0,1},c_{1,2},c_{0,2})=(3,-1,-1,-1)\), a rational 78-decision procedure and a 17-orbit prior certify \(1.3649753<R^\star\le1.364981422\) with primal-dual gap below \(10^{-5}\), while a 15-orbit prior certifies \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}>1.3659\). Thus \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}-R^\star>0.000918578\). For every rational \(t\) with \(|t|\le10^{-5}\), replacing \(c\) by \((3+t,-1-t,-1,-1)\) preserves \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}-R^\star>7\times10^{-4}\).
proposed.justification: The rational separation proves that cross-cluster correlation can lower unrestricted minimax risk, not merely the variance of a selected linear estimator.
proposed.gap: Hull2026's independent-design theorem relies on a no-interference tensorization, and CaiPougetAbadieAiroldi2022 optimizes a conventional estimator; the certified saturation instance permits every measurable estimator on both sides.
proposed.consumer: The result supplies a concrete reason for BairdBohrenMcIntoshOzler2018-style trials to consider correlated saturation labels when robust finite-population MSE is the design criterion.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The displayed instance itself gives \(1\le r_{3,1}=1<3\), \(1\le r_{3,2}=2<3\), and \(r_{3,1}\ne r_{3,2}\). The proof uses bounded outcomes for the contrast-neighborhood Lipschitz bound, but it uses no condition on treated-count entries at other cluster sizes. This replacement removes the two redundant global assumption edges and records the actually used bounded-outcome premise without changing the claim.
